title: How LEGO costs reaches the dashboard
question: How does this repo turn LEGO set prices into the dashboard?
intro: Follow the data from three CSV files through price calculations to the current dashboard. Click an area to inspect its parts, or use Next to follow the path.
subject: Repository as inspected on 23 October 2026
takeaway: The current dashboard is a static page backed by exported set data. Refreshing the source data requires running the database models and the JSON export again.

items.meaning: A plain text table. The project stores LEGO sets, Big Mac prices and stock index values in these files.

sections.title: The data path
sections.intro: Start at the source files, then follow the arrows down to the current website.

areas.name: Source files
areas.about: Three checked-in tables provide set details, burger prices and stock index values.

areas.name: Database models
areas.about: Queries clean the source rows, match prices by date and calculate comparisons.

areas.name: Exported data
areas.about: A Python script copies the final database tables into JSON files.

areas.name: Current website
areas.about: The browser loads set data and draws interactive charts and a searchable table.

parts.name: LEGO sets
parts.about: This table lists sets, pieces, themes, release dates and prices in three currencies.

parts.name: Big Mac prices
parts.about: This table supplies burger prices that let the project compare LEGO costs across time and currencies.

parts.name: Stock index
parts.about: This table supplies S&P 500 values for another way to compare set prices.

parts.name: Clean and match
parts.about: The queries rename columns, fill some missing prices and attach the most recent earlier burger and stock values.

parts.name: Final tables
parts.about: One table has a row per set. The other has yearly medians for the price comparisons.

parts.name: JSON export
parts.about: The script reads both final tables from DuckDB and writes JSON files into the website assets folder.

parts.name: D3 dashboard
parts.about: The page loads set data and calculates cards, time charts, theme bubbles and a searchable table.

parts.name: Earlier Dash app
parts.about: This separate Python app reads an older database copy and draws Plotly charts. The repository describes it as largely abandoned.

start.title: The main idea
start.body: Data preparation happens before someone opens the page. The website reads the prepared file and responds to clicks in the browser.

tour.say: The project starts with set details, Big Mac prices and stock index values in CSV files.
The database queries clean set fields and match each release with earlier price observations.
The final tables hold set comparisons and yearly median values.
The export script copies both final tables into files the browser can read.
The current dashboard loads the set file and draws charts and a searchable table.

sections.title: What happens on a data refresh
sections.intro: The build steps happen before a visitor opens the website.

steps.label: source rows
steps.say: A seed run loads the three CSV tables into DuckDB.

steps.label: cleaned set rows
steps.say: The first queries rename set fields, parse release dates and fill some missing prices.

steps.label: matched price rows
steps.say: The next queries attach the latest Big Mac and stock values dated on or before each release.

steps.label: final results
steps.say: The final queries calculate pieces per currency, per Big Mac and per stock index value.

state.database: Per-set results and yearly medians ready

steps.label: two final tables
steps.say: The export script reads the per-set table and the yearly median table.

steps.label: two JSON files
steps.say: The script writes both tables as JSON files in the website assets folder.

steps.label: load set data
steps.say: When the page opens, JavaScript loads the per-set JSON file.

steps.label: draw charts
steps.say: JavaScript calculates summary numbers and draws the time chart, theme bubbles and raw data table.
steps.screen:
Key metrics and time chart
Theme bubbles and raw data

steps.label: respond to filters
steps.say: Changing a theme or price measure redraws the relevant chart and summary values.

footer: The older Python dashboard and Chart.js page remain in the repository as earlier versions.
